compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
Imagine two staff members in the same restaurant who remember what regular customers usually order and leave clear notes for the next shift. Experience and shared procedures can explain those similarities, whichever type each person identifies with.

The shared S, F and J describe how people take in information, weigh decisions and approach the outside world. Two people may both check the details, weigh how a decision affects others and agree on a plan. They can still arrive at different conclusions.

E/I concerns where attention goes while doing the task. Someone might work through the same question by talking with a colleague or by thinking it through privately. Either approach can involve paying attention to people and to the written record.

### ### ESFJ and ISFJ: making sense of the same handover

In a fictional restaurant handover, two colleagues have the same keys, logs, access to both shifts and two days to prepare. They share responsibility for briefing the incoming team.

Both need to understand the same outstanding issues. One can work through the list in conversation with a colleague, using the answers to clarify what is missing. Another can review the same list privately, organising their questions before talking about it. These are examples of outward and inward attention. Either colleague can do both.

Speaking with both shifts can uncover something absent from the notes. Reviewing the notes can make it easier to spot a gap. Good handover records capture the missing information whichever method revealed it.

compare_blocks.body:
The following fictional scenes illustrate ways of considering information and coordinating a response. Either type can use either approach.

A handover needs clear communication, an accurate stock count and a record the next shift can use. Assign responsibilities according to access, experience and what needs doing.

An answer given before capacity is confirmed can disrupt another booking. A clear refusal can still explain what is available. Those effects depend on the information and commitments, regardless of who gives the answer.

Record the reason for the arrangement and which conditions were checked. The note lets the next shift see what was promised. It gives no evidence about the writer’s type.

### ### ESFJ and ISFJ: following up after the handover

The fictional family treats the doorbell as a way to deal with activity at the door. It cannot monitor a fall in the bathroom or take the place of an agreed way to seek help.

comparison.summary:
ESFJ and ISFJ share Sensing (S), Feeling (F) and Judging (J). They differ only on Extraversion and Introversion (E/I), which describes where attention and energy tend to go. In Myers-Briggs type dynamics, ESFJ leads with extraverted Feeling (Fe), while ISFJ leads with introverted Sensing (Si). Both use Fe in the outside world.

- **Shared S, F and J.** Sensing emphasises concrete details and experience. Feeling weighs values and the effect on people. Judging favours structure and closure in the outside world.
- **The E/I difference.** ESFJ’s E describes a preference for directing attention and energy outward. ISFJ’s I describes a preference for directing them inward. Either type can be talkative with familiar people or want quiet after work.

Under the four-function convention used here, ESFJ is Fe–Si–Ne–Ti and ISFJ is Si–Fe–Ti–Ne. Fe and Si trade the dominant and auxiliary positions. Ne and Ti trade the tertiary and inferior positions. This complete swap depends on the options used for the tertiary functions.

In a handover, either person can speak with colleagues and check the records. Their role, experience and deadline can shape what they do first. Those actions do not identify a type.

compare_blocks.body:

Each row illustrates the direction of attention or a shared aspect of the job. Either colleague can use the approach in either column. There is no way to score the table for type.

compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
Imagine two staff members in the same restaurant who remember what regular customers usually order and leave clear notes for the next shift. Experience and shared procedures can explain those similarities, whichever type each person identifies with.

The shared S, F and J describe how people take in information, weigh decisions and approach the outside world. Two people may both check the details, weigh how a decision affects others and agree on a plan. They can still arrive at different conclusions.

E/I concerns where attention goes while doing the task. Someone might work through the same question by talking with a colleague or by thinking it through privately. Either approach can involve paying attention to people and to the written record.

### ### ESFJ and ISFJ: making sense of the same handover

In a fictional restaurant handover, two colleagues have the same keys, logs, access to both shifts and two days to prepare. They share responsibility for briefing the incoming team.

Both need to understand the same outstanding issues. One can work through the list in conversation with a colleague, using the answers to clarify what is missing. Another can review the same list privately, organising their questions before talking about it. These are examples of outward and inward attention. Either colleague can do both.

Speaking with both shifts can uncover something absent from the notes. Reviewing the notes can make it easier to spot a gap. Good handover records capture the missing information whichever method revealed it.

How someone works on a given day can depend on whether a colleague is available, what the procedure requires and how much time remains. Look across situations where they had a real choice if you want to reflect on E/I.

### ### ESFJ and ISFJ: why Fe and Si switch positions

Both types have F and J, so the model assigns both an outward-facing judging function, Fe. For ESFJ, E makes that function dominant and Si auxiliary. For ISFJ, I makes the inward-facing Si dominant, with Fe in the auxiliary position.

For the stacks shown here, ESFJ’s tertiary Ne is ISFJ’s inferior function, and ISFJ’s tertiary Ti is ESFJ’s inferior function. Each abbreviation keeps its orientation. The positions describe the model, without making claims about speaking order, warmth or attention to detail.

The Myers & Briggs Foundation lists Intuition (Ne or Ni) as ESFJ’s tertiary function and Thinking (Te or Ti) as ISFJ’s. This article uses Ne and Ti, which makes all four abbreviations match across the two stacks. See the [ESFJ profile](/en/personality/esfj) and the [ISFJ profile](/en/personality/isfj) for the individual descriptions.

compare_blocks.body:
The following fictional scenes illustrate ways of considering information and coordinating a response. Either type can use either approach.

A handover needs clear communication, an accurate stock count and a record the next shift can use. Assign responsibilities according to access, experience and what needs doing.

### ### ESFJ and ISFJ: a request for a private room on Friday night

In a fictional restaurant, a regular customer asks for a private room for six on a busy Friday. Both staff members can see the same bookings and capacity, and both are authorised to offer the same options.

Both need to know whether the room is available and what an alternative would mean for the customer. Either can discuss the same options with a colleague or think them through privately before replying. The direction of attention is separate from checking capacity and considering people’s needs.

An answer given before capacity is confirmed can disrupt another booking. A clear refusal can still explain what is available. Those effects depend on the information and commitments, regardless of who gives the answer.

Record the reason for the arrangement and which conditions were checked. The note lets the next shift see what was promised. It gives no evidence about the writer’s type.

### ### ESFJ and ISFJ: following up after the handover

In a fictional handover, both colleagues review the same outstanding items two weeks later. Some issues were mentioned aloud but never recorded. Other notes list an exception without explaining what to do about it.

A conversation can uncover a question the incoming team has not written down. A review of the notes can reveal that nobody has recorded the answer. Either colleague can call the team and document what they learn.

Check that the shared record covers verbal commitments, operating steps, contact details and open questions. Knowing who wrote or raised each item cannot tell you which type they are.

Keep the remaining gaps on one list. Give each an owner and review the updated notes with the people taking over.

### ### ESFJ and ISFJ: discussing a smart doorbell with a relative

In a fictional family, two relatives are considering a smart doorbell for their aunt, who lives alone and has told them about a previous fall. They have the same information and the same role in the discussion. Their aunt decides whether she wants a device.

One question is whether she would welcome a doorbell and who, if anyone, she would want to receive alerts. Another is what the proposed device actually does and who would be available to answer an alert. The same relative can raise both questions, aloud with the family or after taking time to reflect.

The fictional family treats the doorbell as a way to deal with activity at the door. It cannot monitor a fall in the bathroom or take the place of an agreed way to seek help.

If she chooses the doorbell, the family can confirm who receives notifications and test it with her. That checks how the arrangement works. It gives no evidence about who is ESFJ or ISFJ.

An ISFJ can be sociable with familiar people and an ESFJ can look forward to quiet after a shift. E/I describes the usual direction of attention and energy. It does not measure sociability or skill.

sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
Imagine two staff members in the same restaurant who remember what regular customers usually order and leave clear notes for the next shift. Experience and shared procedures can explain those similarities, whichever type each person identifies with.

The shared S, F and J describe how people take in information, weigh decisions and approach the outside world. Two people may both check the details, weigh how a decision affects others and agree on a plan. They can still arrive at different conclusions.

E/I concerns where attention goes while doing the task. Someone might work through the same question by talking with a colleague or by thinking it through privately. Either approach can involve paying attention to people and to the written record.

### ### ESFJ and ISFJ: making sense of the same handover

In a fictional restaurant handover, two colleagues have the same keys, logs, access to both shifts and two days to prepare. They share responsibility for briefing the incoming team.

Both need to understand the same outstanding issues. One can work through the list in conversation with a colleague, using the answers to clarify what is missing. Another can review the same list privately, organising their questions before talking about it. These are examples of outward and inward attention. Either colleague can do both.

Speaking with both shifts can uncover something absent from the notes. Reviewing the notes can make it easier to spot a gap. Good handover records capture the missing information whichever method revealed it.

How someone works on a given day can depend on whether a colleague is available, what the procedure requires and how much time remains. Look across situations where they had a real choice if you want to reflect on E/I.

### ### ESFJ and ISFJ: why Fe and Si switch positions

Both types have F and J, so the model assigns both an outward-facing judging function, Fe. For ESFJ, E makes that function dominant and Si auxiliary. For ISFJ, I makes the inward-facing Si dominant, with Fe in the auxiliary position.

For the stacks shown here, ESFJ’s tertiary Ne is ISFJ’s inferior function, and ISFJ’s tertiary Ti is ESFJ’s inferior function. Each abbreviation keeps its orientation. The positions describe the model, without making claims about speaking order, warmth or attention to detail.

The Myers & Briggs Foundation lists Intuition (Ne or Ni) as ESFJ’s tertiary function and Thinking (Te or Ti) as ISFJ’s. This article uses Ne and Ti, which makes all four abbreviations match across the two stacks. See the [ESFJ profile](/en/personality/esfj) and the [ISFJ profile](/en/personality/isfj) for the individual descriptions.

sections.body_md:
The following fictional scenes illustrate ways of considering information and coordinating a response. Either type can use either approach.

A handover needs clear communication, an accurate stock count and a record the next shift can use. Assign responsibilities according to access, experience and what needs doing.

### ### ESFJ and ISFJ: a request for a private room on Friday night

In a fictional restaurant, a regular customer asks for a private room for six on a busy Friday. Both staff members can see the same bookings and capacity, and both are authorised to offer the same options.

Both need to know whether the room is available and what an alternative would mean for the customer. Either can discuss the same options with a colleague or think them through privately before replying. The direction of attention is separate from checking capacity and considering people’s needs.

An answer given before capacity is confirmed can disrupt another booking. A clear refusal can still explain what is available. Those effects depend on the information and commitments, regardless of who gives the answer.

Record the reason for the arrangement and which conditions were checked. The note lets the next shift see what was promised. It gives no evidence about the writer’s type.

### ### ESFJ and ISFJ: following up after the handover

In a fictional handover, both colleagues review the same outstanding items two weeks later. Some issues were mentioned aloud but never recorded. Other notes list an exception without explaining what to do about it.

A conversation can uncover a question the incoming team has not written down. A review of the notes can reveal that nobody has recorded the answer. Either colleague can call the team and document what they learn.

Check that the shared record covers verbal commitments, operating steps, contact details and open questions. Knowing who wrote or raised each item cannot tell you which type they are.

Keep the remaining gaps on one list. Give each an owner and review the updated notes with the people taking over.

### ### ESFJ and ISFJ: discussing a smart doorbell with a relative

In a fictional family, two relatives are considering a smart doorbell for their aunt, who lives alone and has told them about a previous fall. They have the same information and the same role in the discussion. Their aunt decides whether she wants a device.

One question is whether she would welcome a doorbell and who, if anyone, she would want to receive alerts. Another is what the proposed device actually does and who would be available to answer an alert. The same relative can raise both questions, aloud with the family or after taking time to reflect.

The fictional family treats the doorbell as a way to deal with activity at the door. It cannot monitor a fall in the bathroom or take the place of an agreed way to seek help.

If she chooses the doorbell, the family can confirm who receives notifications and test it with her. That checks how the arrangement works. It gives no evidence about who is ESFJ or ISFJ.

People with either type can keep meticulous notes. Workload, record-keeping habits and the assignment can explain what gets written down.

Customer service can require explaining a decision, checking facts and documenting a promise. Both types can learn and perform those tasks.

Calling a colleague or opening a log first may reflect training, access or time pressure. To reflect on E/I, compare situations in which you could engage outwardly or think privately with similar information available.
